item.title: 'Arrival' at 10: Denis Villeneuve's alien visitation classic that reminded us it's good to talk
item.description:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In " Star Trek ", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication. But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun. The film's journey to the big screen began when a screenwriter best known for his work on horror franchises such as "Final Destination", "A Nightmare on Elm Street" and "The Thing" read a short story in an online magazine. Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. One in particular, the Nebula Award-winning "Story of Your Life", piqued his interest. "It had a very profound emotional effect on me," he reminisced to Deadline . "I was in tears, and I was both heartbroken and uplifted. My head was just full of big ideas. I had to walk around the block a couple of times afterward and just hug my friends. The next day, I was like, 'Oh god, I want to give this to other people.'" So when 21 Laps (the production company that later went on to make " Stranger Things ") invited Heisserer to discuss possible future projects, the writer mentioned "Story of Your Life". The producers were also smitten. (Image credit: Paramount Pictures) "I was so excited, but I had that dread that a lot of producers get, which is, 'Are the rights available?'" 21 Laps' Dan Levine told the Hollywood Gold podcast. "You read something that blows you away, and then you find there aren't the rights, and there's no chance, you have to move on. So we were trying to track down this Ted Chiang, and he had no agent. He had a day job. He was impossible to find, so we started the hunt for Ted Chiang." An up-and-coming Canadian director named Denis Villeneuve h
item.dc:creator: Richard Edwards
item.content:encoded:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In " Star Trek ", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication. But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun. The film's journey to the big screen began when a screenwriter best known for his work on horror franchises such as "Final Destination", "A Nightmare on Elm Street" and "The Thing" read a short story in an online magazine. Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. One in particular, the Nebula Award-winning "Story of Your Life", piqued his interest. "It had a very profound emotional effect on me," he reminisced to Deadline . "I was in tears, and I was both heartbroken and uplifted. My head was just full of big ideas. I had to walk around the block a couple of times afterward and just hug my friends. The next day, I was like, 'Oh god, I want to give this to other people.'" So when 21 Laps (the production company that later went on to make " Stranger Things ") invited Heisserer to discuss possible future projects, the writer mentioned "Story of Your Life". The producers were also smitten. (Image credit: Paramount Pictures) "I was so excited, but I had that dread that a lot of producers get, which is, 'Are the rights available?'" 21 Laps' Dan Levine told the Hollywood Gold podcast. "You read something that blows you away, and then you find there aren't the rights, and there's no chance, you have to move on. So we were trying to track down this Ted Chiang, and he had no agent. He had a day job. He was impossible to find, so we started the hunt for Ted Chiang." An up-and-coming Canadian director named Denis Villeneuve had also found his way on to 21 Laps' radar after his 2010 French-language drama "Incendies" earned rave reviews and an Academy Award nomination. He told the producers that he'd always wanted to direct a science fiction film — a hint of things to come? — and they showed him "Story of Your Life". (Image credit: Paramount Pictures) He was also drawn to the story, while the now-located Chiang was suitably impressed by the director's work on "Incendies" to make a deal for the rights. And with Amy Adams also interested in playing the lead role of linguist Dr Louise Banks, the film that would eventually become "Arrival" was ready to proceed — or, at least, it would be once Villeneuve had completed his first three Hollywood movies, "Prisoners" (2013), "Enemy" (2013) and "Sicario" (2015). With 12 alien spaceships arriving simultaneously around the globe, "Arrival"'s poster-friendly elevator pitch could almost have been borrowed from " Independence Day ". Indeed, the question of whether these whisper-quiet, chocolate button-shaped craft belong to the " Day the Earth Stood Still " / "Close Encounters" friendly extraterrestrial camp, or have the invasion of planet Earth on their minds is a mystery the world's governments are desperate to solve. "Denis didn't really see this as an alien invasion movie — more an alien arrival movie," producer Aaron Ryder told SFX magazine. "What would be the protocols that were in place? How would they be implemented? How would people react? What would the government be doing? What would the news organisations be saying? That was the tone and the texture, which is established right up front." (Image credit: Paramount Pictures) These Hollywood blockbuster components were not part of "Story of Your Life". But even though Heisserer's script was not a direct translation of Chiang's tale, he retained the most important bits — namely Dr Banks' efforts to establish a means of communication with seven-legged extraterrestrial heptapods, and the profound effect their language has on her perception of time. Designed by Carlos Huante, the heptapods themselves are like giant elongated hands, alien visitors light years away from the "Star Trek" tradition of actors with a few ridges glued to their foreheads. Like the evil 456 in " Torchwood: Children of Earth ", they're enclosed in gaseous chambers and make sounds imperceptible to the human ear. This, however, is where "Arrival" gets really interesting. Working alongside physicist colleague Dr Ian Donnelly (Jeremy Renner), Banks gradually exchanges foundational vocabulary with two heptapods they name Abbott and Costello. They discover that the alien visitors use a sophisticated written language of circular "logograms", squirted into their atmosphere as if it were sentient squid ink. (Image credit: Paramount Pictures) "The idea in the short story is of circular language that has no beginning and no end," Villeneuve explained in an interview with IndieWire . "We were looking for no relation to any human language. I had to figure out how to produce logograms from my aliens while avoiding being long and boring. The sounds were an expression of their emotions, with more intellect coming from the signs. This beautiful species uses written language as their first means of expression instead of movement or gesture. They produce words out of their bodies." But Banks and Donnelly's research project has a purpose. With the world's military on high alert — and, ironically, struggling to communicate — they need to work out how to ask the aliens a fundamental question: Why are you here? The heptapods' answer — "offer weapon" — is tantalizingly ambiguous. Are they planning to attack? Or is, as Banks suggests, 'weapon' simply being used as a synonym for 'tool'? SPOILERS AHEAD (Image credit: Paramount Pictures) Aside from a bomb planted on the heptapod ship by a rogue US soldier, "Arrival" is mostly free from the big-budget explosions that are part-and-parcel of most alien visitation movies. Instead, the film's denouement delivers a twist — the crux of Chiang's story — that rivals "The Sixth Sense", "Fight Club" and "The Prestige" in its audacious sleight of hand. It turns out the "weapon" in question is actually the heptapod language, which, thanks to their non-linear perception of time, gives speakers a unique perspective on the past, present, and future. Therefore, those scenes we assumed to be flash backs to the life and tragic death of Louise's daughter, Hannah, are actually flash forwards , as her increased understanding of heptapod-speak gives her memories of a life she hasn't yet lived. Villeneuve put on multiple test screenings to ensure the big reveals hit properly. "I wanted to screen it with people who knew nothing about the project," he said. "What we discovered is when someone in the audience felt too lost — if intellectually they were not engaged — the ending was less powerful from an emotional point of view. So we tried to give as f

item.title: Hollandia Yoghurt Highlights Versatility in Nigeria’s Evolving Food Culture
item.description: Hollandia Yoghurt is showcasing the different ways consumers can enjoy the product as part of everyday meals and snacks through its “Yoghurt It How You Want It ” campaign, while reaffirming its commitment to delivering quality products to Nigerian consumers. The campaign highlights how Hollandia Yoghurt can be enjoyed beyond a standalone beverage, featuring in breakfast options, snacks, smoothies and simple recipes. This consumer-focused approach is underpinned by Hollandia’s commitment to quality, with products carrying the masterbrand made with careful consideration and best-in-class quality processes. Speaking on the campaign, Olugbenga Akindele , Category Head, Dairy, said the initiative combines the brand’s focus on quality with an invitation for consumers to explore different ways to enjoy Hollandia Yoghurt. “At Hollandia, quality remains central to our commitment to consumers. Our products are made with careful consideration and best-in-class quality processes, reflecting our commitment to delivering products consumers can enjoy with confidence. Through our ‘Yoghurt It How You Want It’ campaign, we want consumers to discover more ways to enjoy Hollandia Yoghurt, whether as part of breakfast, a quick snack or their favourite food combinations, ” he said. Hollandia Yoghurt can be paired with popular snacks such as meat pies, sausage rolls and puff-puff, or combined with fruits and granola to create breakfast bowls and parfaits. It can also be blended with fruits to prepare smoothies or incorporated into selected recipes. The range offers consumers different flavour options to suit their preferences. Hollandia Strawberry brings a fruity taste to breakfast bowls and smoothies, while Hollandia Vanilla offers a creamy flavour for combinations such as pancakes, granola and parfaits. Hollandia Plain Sweetened provides another option for pairing with fruits, nuts and other toppings. Available in 315ml and 1L packs, Hollandia Yoghurt caters to different consumption occasions, from individual refreshment to household use and food preparation. Through the “Yoghurt It How You Want It ” campaign, Hollandia is encouraging consumers to explore different ways to incorporate Hollandia Yoghurt into their routines, with product quality remaining central to the brand’s commitment to Nigerian households. item.title: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today
item.description: null LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13). After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall. "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour. The space shuttle Endeavour. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) "There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience." Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life. The new Endeavour exhibit features a replica launch tower, from which you can look down at the shuttle. (Image credit: Future) There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with. As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top. A replica of the space shuttle Endeavour's flight deck. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you). This is the abbreviated description, but know that if you are visiting the California Science Center, you will want to budget a serious amount of time to explore all that this new center has to offer. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall. "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour. The space shuttle Endeavour. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) "There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience." Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life. The new Endeavour exhibit features a replica launch tower, from which you can look down at the shuttle. (Image credit: Future) There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with. As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top. A replica of the space shuttle Endeavour's flight deck. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you). This is the abbreviated description, but know that if you are visiting the California Science Center, you will want to budget a serious amount of time to explore all that this new center has to offer. External view of the replica Endeavour flight deck at the new California Science Center exhibit. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) The new air and space center is designed for all ages, and for civilians and astronauts alike. For instance, looking at Endeavour spurred some memories for Reisman: He reflected on his time aboard the shuttle and his time as an astronaut and pinpointed specific places on the shuttle that played important roles in his mission. "I'm looking at handrails that I held onto during a spacewalk ," he said. "They're the same handrails. My hand was in the glove, but it was wrapped around those handrails. And I practiced for a long time exactly how I was going to do that, how I was going to root my tether, and all that kind of stuff. And I get to stand [here] now. When you go up the elevator there, you can actually have a direct view of those handrails, and every time I see that, I'm thinking about that spacewalk." But you don't need to have completed a spacewalk to get that view. And, as of today, the general public is welcome to visit the museum, which is free to the public — as is the new aerospace center with its Endeavour exhibit. However, due to the excitement over this new center opening, you will need to make a reservation online to attend. And, while the museum is free to the public, there is a cost associated with reserving slots during these busy first few days.

item.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
item.description: null Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up. But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes. What's happening and when to look You can easily see the Pleiades as a bright misty patch in your peripheral vision during winter. (Image credit: Haitong Yu via Getty Images) The Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns. In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun , but their stars are about 625 million years old. The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Big Dipper /Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness. That makes M45 much more interesting to me than a simple tick-box target. So tonight, don't just find the Pleiades — count them. item.content:encoded: null Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up. But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes. What's happening and when to look You can easily see the Pleiades as a bright misty patch in your peripheral vision during winter. (Image credit: Haitong Yu via Getty Images) The Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns. In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun , but their stars are about 625 million years old. The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Big Dipper /Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness. That makes M45 much more interesting to me than a simple tick-box target. So tonight, don't just find the Pleiades — count them. How and when I'm watching it Counting the stars you can see in the Pleiades is a fun way to test your naked-eye observing skills. (Image credit: Siesei / 500px via Getty Images) I'm going to run my Pleiades eye test in stages. First, I'll step outside and look almost immediately. I'll count the individual stars I can distinguish without spending ages convincing myself about marginal ones. Then I'll wait. After about 10 minutes (without looking at my phone or bright outdoor lights, of course), I'll count again. Full dark adaptation takes considerably longer, but even 10 minutes can make an obvious difference when you've just come from a brightly lit house. I'll then try my trusty 10x50 binoculars. This is where the experiment stops being subtle. The little naked-eye knot of brightness suddenly becomes a field filled with stars. The Pleiades don't just become brighter through binoculars. Their whole character changes because stars that were below my naked-eye threshold appear. I'll also use the averted vision technique, looking slightly to one side rather than directly at M45. It's one of the best demonstrations of the technique, with its fainter stars seemingly popping into view as your more light-sensitive peripheral vision takes over. Stargazer's corner: November 13-19, 2026 It's a good week to see "Earthshine" on the crescent moon. (Image credit: Jeff Schneiderman via Getty Images) The moon is returning to the evening sky this week, waxing from a thin crescent toward first quarter. It reaches first quarter around Nov. 17, so moonlight becomes progressively more noticeable during the first half of the night. Look southwest during twilight, and you'll see the beautiful sight of a crescent moon sporting Earthshine, sunlight reflected from Earth onto the moon's night side. Overnight, Nov. 15-16, don't miss Mars and Jupiter in conjunction. The two planets will appear just over a degree apart, rising in the east during the evening before climbing high into the southern sky in the hours before sunrise. The following night, Nov. 17-18, the Leonid meteor shower peaks. This is one shower where staying up later actually matters. Leo, the constellation containing the shower's radiant, doesn't rise until late, so the better opportunity comes after midnight and toward the predawn hours. Asterism of the week: The Kids Auriga is one of the easiest constellations to find in the Northern Hemisphere's winter night sky. (Image credit: Starry Night) Auriga, "the Charioteer," is easy to see in the northeastern and eastern sky during November evenings, but have you spied the asterism close to its brightest star, Capella? It's known as the "Goat Star," though its Latin name is the diminutive of capra, meaning "little she-goat." The reason is esoteric — Capella represents Amalthea, the mythological goat that suckled the infant Zeus — but there is a neat asterism (shape of stars) nearby that suddenly makes sense. Close to Capella is a triangle of faint stars that are known as The Kids — Epsilon, Zeta and Eta Aurigae — traditionally imagined as the offspring of Capella. It's one of those little patterns that makes a constellation much easier to recognize.

item.title: Nigerian-Born Shirley Emehelu Makes History as New Jersey’s First Immigrant Lieutenant Governor
item.description: Shirley U. Emehelu, New Jersey’s fifth Lieutenant Governor and Secretary of State. Photo Credit: Official Site of New Jersey A Nigerian-born legal leader has made history in New Jersey. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill has officially appointed Nigerian-American Shirley U . Emehelu as the state’s fifth Lieutenant Governor and Secretary of State . Sworn in at the New Jersey Statehouse in Trenton on 9 November 2026, Emehelu has made double history in the process—becoming New Jersey’s first immigrant Lieutenant Governor and forming part of the state’s first all-women Governor–Lieutenant Governor team. Born in Nigeria before moving to the United States at the age of three, Emehelu brings an extraordinary record of public service and legal excellence to New Jersey’s second-highest executive office. Before this historic appointment, she served as Acting State Comptroller , leading key efforts to combat fraud, waste, and abuse while protecting taxpayer funds and strengthening government accountability, and also stepped in as Acting Secretary of State to oversee New Jersey’s elections. Her public sector résumé also includes a two-year tenure as Executive Assistant Attorney General of New Jersey, where she served as the third-ranking official in the New Jersey Attorney General’s Office. In that role, she directly counselled the Attorney General, coordinated oversight for more than 500 attorneys within the Division of Law—New Jersey’s largest legal office—and directed civil defence and enforcement matters across civil rights, environmental protection, labour and consumer protections, data privacy, and firearms safety. New Jersey Lieutenant Governor Shirley U. Emehelu, part of the state’s first all-women Governor–Lieutenant Governor team. Photo Credit: Shirley U. Emehelu/LinkedIn Earlier in her career, Emehelu spent nine years at the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Jersey, serving as Chief of Asset Recovery and Anti-Money Laundering, where she prosecuted complex financial fraud cases and oversaw statewide asset forfeiture and victim restitution programmes. She also practised in the private sector as a member of the White-Collar Criminal Defense and Government Investigations Group at CSG Law, co-leading the firm’s Banking and Finance Group, after clerking for the Honourable James R.Spencer in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. An alumna of Yale University (where she earned her B.A.) and Yale Law School (where she earned her J.D.), Emehelu is a proud resident of Montclair, New Jersey, where she and her husband, Ike , raised their two children, Nnamdi and Amara . Speaking on the appointment, Governor Mikie Sherrill praised Emehelu’s track record in accountability and public service, noting : From prosecuting financial fraud and rooting out waste and abuse, to defending civil rights and protecting consumers, Shirley has fought for New Jersey families at every step of her career. Shirley also maintains strong leadership

She also practised in the private sector as a member of the White-Collar Criminal Defense and Government Investigations Group at CSG Law, co-leading the firm’s Banking and Finance Group, after clerking for the Honourable James R.Spencer in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. An alumna of Yale University (where she earned her B.A.) and Yale Law School (where she earned her J.D.), Emehelu is a proud resident of Montclair, New Jersey, where she and her husband, Ike , raised their two children, Nnamdi and Amara . Speaking on the appointment, Governor Mikie Sherrill praised Emehelu’s track record in accountability and public service, noting : From prosecuting financial fraud and rooting out waste and abuse, to defending civil rights and protecting consumers, Shirley has fought for New Jersey families at every step of her career. Shirley also maintains strong leadership at the Secretary of State’s office after successfully overseeing the smooth administration of our elections last week. She pairs the highest ethical standards with the same tenacity to run toward our toughest challenges, and I am proud to have her by my side as we work to deliver for the people of New Jersey. Accepting the historic appointment, Lieutenant Governor Shirley U. Emehelu shared: I am honoured by Governor Sherrill’s trust and the opportunity to serve the people of New Jersey as Lieutenant Governor. I’ve spent my career upholding the law, protecting families, and rooting out fraud, abuse, and corruption. As Lieutenant Governor and continuing my role as Secretary of State, I’ll bring that same tenacity to lowering costs, expanding opportunity for every community, and ensuring government delivers for the people we serve. The post Nigerian-Born Shirley Emehelu Makes History as New Jersey’s First Immigrant Lieutenant Governor appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: 'Martian Isolation' is an upcoming sci-fi survival horror game that looks like 'The Martian' and 'Event Horizon' had a horrific child
item.description: null "Martian Isolation" is an upcoming single-player, first-person survival horror game that's just been revealed with a suitably creepy launch trailer. And yes, it does look an awful lot like " The Martian ," doesn't it? There's a lot of survival gameplay on display here that mirrors Mark Watney's tale of survival on the Red Planet, as your stranded protagonist is forced to explore the Martian surface to acquire resources, grow plants, and repair their base. That comparison to Andy Weir's sci-fi masterpiece does fall away as you get further into the trailer, though, when the horror part of the game's description comes into play: Flickering lights, creepy figures stalking the halls of your Martian habitat, and blood dripping from the walls. Oh yeah, that's some good creepy sci-fi horror right there. It's giving " Event Horizon ", and that's always getting a thumbs-up from me. There's no release date scheduled at this time, with the 'Martian Isolation' Steam page simply listing it as "coming soon," though the YouTube trailer description does say it "will be available on Steam in 2027". You can't pre-order yet, but if this looks like your jam, you can add it to your wishlist. Beyond that, we know shockingly little about this title. It's the debut game from Golden Milestone Studio, but there's very little information out there beyond a name. The latest blog post on the game's Steam page says that they're a "small team," but what we've seen so far is encouraging. There seems to be a pronounced split between the survival and horror elements of the game along the day/night cycle. Daytime sees you exploring the Martian surface, smashing rocks, cleaning solar panels, and doing sick jumps on a quad bike. The psychological torment only begins once the sun goes down (they mostly come out at night … mostly), as your character starts encountering cosmic horrors and weird naked zombie men. Mars rover, nice. Golden Milestone Studio Spacesuits, check. Golden Milestone Studio Crafting, of course. Golden Milestone Studio OH SWEET JESUS! Get it away, get it away. Golden Milestone Studio OK, we're good. Mining, cool. Golden Milestone Studio Riding a quad bike on Mars, yes please. Golden Milestone Studio Growing potatoes on Mars, just like that guy in the movie. Golden Milestone Studio Opening a box with power tools, seems excessive but sure. Golden Milestone Studio NOPE! Nope, nope, nope, I'm out! Golden Milestone Studio Are they hallucinations, or is there some malevolent presence hiding in the blood-red sands of Mars ? I'm always looking for new ways to shatter my psyche and possibly soil my pants, so I'll be keeping a close eye on this one. In the meantime, I do need to get back and finish " Routine ." I left my character hiding under a desk months ago, and I haven't been brave enough to go back. As Mama always said, you can't have any Martian horror until you finish your lunar horror first.

item.title: Astronomers trace mystery radio signals back to cosmic odd couple of white dwarf and sun-like star
item.description: null Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star. The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153. GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs. The unusual system consists of a small and highly energetic white dwarf pulsar, orbiting a much larger star similar to our sun. (Image credit: ICRAR) "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, said in a statement . "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself." The pulses seen by the team also allowed them to detect stellar flares erupting on the sun-like star. "As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence,' which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface," team member Natasha Hurley-Walker of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), Curtin University, Australia, said. "It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away." South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope. (Image credit: South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO)) Hurley-Walker and the team at ICRAR have been at the cutting edge of rare star systems like this. "We detected this system in a large survey using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia," Hurley-Walker said. "We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position." After the radio telescopes detected this LPT, it was confirmed using the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The visible light follow-up of Keck also confirmed that the star in GPM J071507−114153 was a G-type star, just like the sun. "As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence,' which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface," team member Natasha Hurley-Walker of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), Curtin University, Australia, said. "We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position." After the radio telescopes detected this LPT, it was confirmed using the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The visible light follow-up of Keck also confirmed that the star in GPM J071507−114153 was a G-type star, just like the sun. MeerKAT and the MWA are both precursors for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the world’s largest and most sensitive radio telescope project. That means the future is bright for LPTs. "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKA telescopes are completely built," McSweeney said. The team's research was published on Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

item.title: Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down
item.description: Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30. Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. S ome 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names. Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ , users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com , with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of. It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will. Mozilla told The Register : "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider." It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere. Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now. Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

item.title: Netflix’s ‘Ray Gunn’ gets 2nd trailer, and we're hyped for this animated sci-fi noir from ‘Incredibles’ director Brad Bird
item.description: null Dreaming of a bright and shiny future filled with personal jet packs, levitating autos, and automated gadgets straight out of " The Jetsons ?" Add in a gritty mystery, a notorious private eye, double-crossing aliens, and a bombshell diva framed for a killing, and you’ve got the perfect recipe for "Ray Gunn." Oscar-winning director Brad Bird ("The Incredibles," "Ratatouille") returns to our screens with his new big-budget animated sci-fi project, " Ray Gunn ," and this latest trailer has us primed. "In Metropia, a gigantic city in an alternate future as seen from 1939, private eye Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell) is drawn into a case involving aliens, murder, and a multimedia starlet named Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson)," states the official synopsis. Netflix Films and Skydance Animation's "Ray Gunn" is a stylistic pastiche of classic film noir tropes populated by down-and-out detectives and femme fatales living in the inspiring air of technological optimism viewed through a pre-war America lens. Think "The Fifth Element" meets "Who Framed Roger Rabbit?" and "The Maltese Falcon," and you’re going to be close to this sci-fi whodunnit's vibe, which is intended for more mature audiences and rated PG. "The Incredibles'" Brad Bird serves up a sci-fi detective tale in "Ray Gunn" (Image credit: Netflix) This energetic new preview is locked and loaded with dazzling visuals by Cinesite, freaky creatures, streamlined flying cars, and a blistering pace. And if you listen very closely, The B-52s' "Planet Claire" can be heard playing in the background, which is one of the touchstones that inspired Bird to begin his 36-year journey to bring "Ray Gunn" to life. Was it worth the wait? We'll have to find out. Also starring the vocal talents of Tom Waits, Bobby Cannavale, Alan Tudyk, Matt Berry, and Michelle Rodriguez, "Ray Gunn" opens in select theaters and 70mm screenings Dec. 4. After that, it lands on Netflix on Dec. 18... a date you might want to circle on your calendar, as that’s also the release slot for " Avengers: Doomsday " and " Dune: Part 3. " It's going to be a busy day for sci-fi fans. "Strap in, buster!" Watch Ray Gunn on Netflix on Dec 18: Standard with ads: $8.99/month Standard: $19.99/month Premium (4K): $26.99/month

item.title: I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review
item.description: null Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a new telescope. Finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit. At 25 lbs (11.33 kg), the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a relative heavyweight. Jamie Carter The supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces provide 30x and 75x magnification, respectively, but are obvious candidates for future upgrades. Jamie Carter The StarSense Explorer smartphone dock uses a small mirror. Jamie Carter It was a stunning view, and exactly the kind of experience a beginner needs from a first telescope. There was no frustration and no wondering whether I was looking in the right place. StarSense took me straight there — but, crucially, I moved the telescope myself. I’ve always liked that combination of hand-holding and DIY observing that Celestron’s StarSense tech gives you. I’m less convinced by the tabletop telescope it’s attached to. Although this $599 RRP (£379) model is significantly smaller than the Celestron StarSense Explorer 8-inch Dobsonian telescope I’ve previously reviewed, it still weighs 25 lbs (11.33 kg). You need to place it on something sturdy before you can use it comfortably. After living with it in my backyard, I’m not convinced the tabletop format is the advantage it initially appears to be. An iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted securely into the StarSense Explorer smartphone dock during testing. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) What StarSense Explorer does well The Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian comes with a red dot finder for manual navigation. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) I’ve used Celestron’s StarSense Explorer system on a variety of telescopes and have always been impressed by how easy this type of smartphone navigation is to use. The technology works just as well here and, for me, it remains one of the best ways of making a traditional optical telescope accessible to a complete beginner. This isn’t a computerized GoTo telescope. There are no motors to slew across the sky automatically and no tracking system to keep an object centered. Instead, a smartphone sits in a dock attached to the telescope, and its camera looks at the sky via a small mirror. An iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted securely into the StarSense Explorer smartphone dock during testing. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) What StarSense Explorer does well The Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian comes with a red dot finder for manual navigation. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) I’ve used Celestron’s StarSense Explorer system on a variety of telescopes and have always been impressed by how easy this type of smartphone navigation is to use. The technology works just as well here and, for me, it remains one of the best ways of making a traditional optical telescope accessible to a complete beginner. This isn’t a computerized GoTo telescope. There are no motors to slew across the sky automatically and no tracking system to keep an object centered. Instead, a smartphone sits in a dock attached to the telescope, and its camera looks at the sky via a small mirror. Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app analyzes the reflections of the stars it sees, works out exactly where the telescope is pointing and tells you which direction to push it to reach the object you want to observe. My iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted perfectly into the dock, and the initial alignment process was identical to what I’d used before. Once that was done, I used StarSense to find the Pleiades (M45), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Double Cluster in Perseus and Saturn. It worked every time, with the target appearing in the eyepiece when the app told me I had reached it. I can find all of those objects without an app, but that’s not really the point. Beginners often struggle to translate a star chart or an astronomy app into actual telescope movements. StarSense gives you confidence that you’re heading in the right direction while still requiring you to operate it physically. That makes it a useful way to learn the night sky. After repeatedly pushing the telescope from one familiar object to another, you begin to understand how everything fits together. That’s very different from pressing a button and watching a GoTo or smart telescope move itself, and it’s why I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, even on a relatively wide-field telescope like this one. The 5.9-inch mirror produces lovely wide-field views A Newtonian reflector uses curved and flat mirrors to gather and focus light into an eyepiece. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) The StarSense system may be the headline feature, but the reason to buy any Dobsonian is aperture. This one uses a 150mm (5.9-inch) parabolic primary mirror with a 750mm focal length and a relatively fast f/5 focal ratio. That combination gives it fairly low-power, wide-field views that are particularly well suited to large star clusters. The Pleiades was one of my favorite views. At 30x through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, the telescope gave me a sharp field of stars and a particularly good view of what I call “Carter’s Whip” — the curving line of stars running through the cluster. I saw little obvious softness towards the edges, and focusing was straightforward. The 150mm f/5 optics are particularly well suited to wide-field views of objects such as the Pleiades. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) was a different proposition. From my light-polluted backyard, I could see Andromeda’s bright core, but not its outskirts or its satellite galaxies. That’s largely a consequence of observing a galaxy from a city, not a criticism of a 150mm telescope, but it’s a useful reminder of what visual astronomy is actually like. Don’t expect the colorful, detailed views of galaxies and nebulas you see in astrophotos, such as the stacked images a smart telescope can give you. Saturn was more rewarding, but I would have liked more magnification when the seeing was this good. Add a Barlow lens if planets are a priority — it can double the magnification of any eyepiece you use it with. Celestron StarSense Explorer Dobsonians are available with apertures up to 12 inches. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Overall, I was impressed by the telescope’s optics. The views were sharp and contrast-y, and there’s enough aperture here to make a serious start in visual astronomy. However, the two supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces are decidedly entry-level — and obvious candidates for upgrading in the medium term. The focuser is a weak point. It’s a fairly basic 1.25-inch rack-and-pinion design, but I noticed some wobble and vibration while using it. That’s a shame because the focuser is one of the parts of a telescope you constantly interact with, and something smoother and more precise would make the entire instrument feel more accomplished. The supplied red dot finder is of fairly basic quality. Jamie Carter A tabletop telescope needs the right table A grab handle makes it easy to move the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian into position. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) The tabletop design isn’t necessarily as convenient as it sounds. I expected this scope to feel considerably more convenient than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Dobsonian. The base has built-in grab handles, but the assembled telescope's shape and weight make it awkward to lift onto a table — I certainly wouldn’t recommend it to anyone with a bad back. You could move the optical tube and base separately, but that starts to cancel out the convenience of owning a relatively compact tabletop telescope. You also need to choose your table carefully. It has to be sturdy enough not to introduce vibrations, but not so large that you have to stretch across it to reach the eyepiece as the telescope points to different parts of the sky. I found myself bending and stretching into some awkward positions. Once it’s in position, the Dobsonian mount worked well. The balance was good, and I didn't need to adjust the altitude tension, while the movements offered a useful mix of resistance and fluidity as I followed StarSense around the sky. At 75x, however, keeping Saturn centered was more difficult than I expected. It was easy to over-nudge the telescope

item.title: Astronaut Suni Williams rides through NYC as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade | Space photo of the day for Nov. 13, 2026
item.description: null NASA astronaut Suni Williams rides through New York City as the Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: Photo by Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images) New Yorkers got a space-y surprise on Wednesday (Nov. 11): Retired NASA astronaut and U.S. Navy Captain Sunita "Suni" Williams rolled down 5th Avenue in the back of a classic convertible wrapped in patriotic decals as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade. What is it? On Wednesday, New York City's 107th annual Veterans Day Parade made its way through Manhattan to the cheers and respectful nods of thousands of onlookers. The parade is an annual tradition on the holiday, which honors veterans of the U.S. armed forces. As part of the parade, veterans, active-duty soldiers, firefighters, marching bands, youth cadets and more march through the city and honor those who have served and sacrificed in the U.S. military. This year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join New Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event. Why is it incredible? Williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025 . She spent 608 days in space during her astronaut career, the second-most by an American astronaut behind Peggy Whitson , who racked up 695. Williams also had an extensive career in the U.S. Navy. She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017. During this time, Williams supported relief efforts following Hurricane Andrew, trained within the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and gained a wealth of further experience flying as a military pilot. Williams is part of a longstanding tradition of astronauts serving in the U.S. military. From test pilots to naval officers and more, there's a strong link between the U.S. armed forces and NASA's astronaut program.

item.title: FWIFT 2026 Convention Communique: Industry Leaders Charge Women in Media to Embrace Cross-Border Growth
item.description: The Forum for Women in Film and Television Nigeria (FWIFT) successfully concluded its 2026 annual convention on Thursday, October 29, at the historic Glover Memorial Hall in Lagos, Nigeria. Convening under the theme “One Industry, Many Voices: Building Together,” the afternoon brought together over 200 practitioners from several sectors including; film, television, radio, advertising, and digital media to connect, share insights, and build mutual agency. Supported by the African Women’s Development Fund (AWDF) , the convention featured a keynote address by cultural curator Sandra Mbanefo Obiago , interactive panel sessions, break-out workshops, speed networking, and a flagship fireside chat titled “The Cross Over: A Career Beyond Borders.” The event drew leading voices from across the creative economy, including media executive Kadaria Ahmed , filmmaker Biodun Stephens, media personality Gbemi Olateru-Olagbegi, executive director Rosemary Egabor-Afolahan, and director Esosa Osagiede. Key takeaways and actionable resolutions from the convention sessions emphasized resilience, strategic partnerships, and structural evolution: Embrace Bold Collaboration and Risk-Taking: Speakers urged media professionals to shed apprehension around institutional partnerships. As highlighted during the panel discussions: “Do not allow fear of failing stop you from asking for help, do your due diligence on the people you want to partner with then go for it. If it does not work, do not stop, get up and go again.” Adaptability as a Survival Imperative: In an era of rapid technological and digital shifts across broadcast and film, participants were reminded of the absolute necessity of evolution: “If you don’t change with the times, you will grow stale.” Deconstructing Industry Myths: Addressing professional dynamics, panelists challenged antiquated narratives regarding female competition, affirming that systemic progress relies on solidarity: “Women work well with women, it is a myth that they do not.” FWIFT’s leadership noted that the conversations at Glover Memorial Hall mark a critical step toward cementing cross-sector alliances. The forum remains committed to translating these insights into actionable frameworks, mentorship programs, and policy advocacy for women shaping the future of African media. For more information on upcoming FWIFT initiatives, programs, and future events, visit the official website or follow @fwiftnigeria on social media. About FWIFT Nigeria The Forum For Women in Film and Television Nigeria (FWIFT) is a professional organization dedicated to empowering Nigerian women in screen-based, audio, and digital media through advocacy, skill acquisition, mentorship, and strategic networking. Media Contact: Forum of Women in Film and Television Nigeria (FWIFT) Email: fwiftnigeria@gmail.com | Website . BellaNaija is a Media Partner for FWIFT The post FWIFT 2026 Convention Communique: Industry Leaders Charge Women in Media to Embrace Cross-Border Growth

item.title: Double-catch drama: Why Starship's Flight 15 is so important to SpaceX
item.description: null Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap . Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the company eyes hourly launches by 2030. SpaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship 's 15th flight, which will lift off from the company's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad. "If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description . The 75-minute Flight 15 launch window opens today at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), and a number of Starship firsts are planned for early in the flight. For example, while SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy boosters and reused two of them to date, the first attempt to catch a next-gen Super Heavy "V3" vehicle will come today, around 6.5 minutes after liftoff. If the Ship upper stage gets the go-ahead for orbital insertion, it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites — designed especially for use on Starship — into low Earth orbit (LEO), starting about 35 minutes after launch. Then, 21 hours later, if "internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions" for a return to Starbase and catch are met — including on-orbit assessment of Ship's heat shield by three of the V3 satellites — SpaceX will attempt to recover the orbital upper stage. This landmark try will follow the first-ever Ship reentry over inhabited areas, as the vehicle will maneuver its way over sparsely populated regions of northern Mexico and southern Texas. (On previous missions, Ship has splashed down in the open ocean.) It will head back to Starbase and make a bellyflop maneuver as it descends to the site's Pad 2 before flipping itself vertical, ready for embrace of the launch tower's waiting mechanical arms. "SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact," Elon Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Nov. 6 . "This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary." Composite photo showing the Super Heavy booster of SpaceX's Starship megarocket coming in for a landing on the launch mount on Oct. 13, 2024. item.dc:creator: Andrew Jones
item.content:encoded: null Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap . Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the company eyes hourly launches by 2030. SpaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship 's 15th flight, which will lift off from the company's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad. "If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description . The 75-minute Flight 15 launch window opens today at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), and a number of Starship firsts are planned for early in the flight. For example, while SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy boosters and reused two of them to date, the first attempt to catch a next-gen Super Heavy "V3" vehicle will come today, around 6.5 minutes after liftoff. If the Ship upper stage gets the go-ahead for orbital insertion, it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites — designed especially for use on Starship — into low Earth orbit (LEO), starting about 35 minutes after launch. Then, 21 hours later, if "internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions" for a return to Starbase and catch are met — including on-orbit assessment of Ship's heat shield by three of the V3 satellites — SpaceX will attempt to recover the orbital upper stage. This landmark try will follow the first-ever Ship reentry over inhabited areas, as the vehicle will maneuver its way over sparsely populated regions of northern Mexico and southern Texas. (On previous missions, Ship has splashed down in the open ocean.) It will head back to Starbase and make a bellyflop maneuver as it descends to the site's Pad 2 before flipping itself vertical, ready for embrace of the launch tower's waiting mechanical arms. "SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact," Elon Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Nov. 6 . "This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary." Composite photo showing the Super Heavy booster of SpaceX's Starship megarocket coming in for a landing on the launch mount on Oct. 13, 2024. (Image credit: SpaceX via X) The catch Half of the system is already proven. With catching and reflying boosters largely established, the next and unprecedented step is catching Ship. This is no easy task. The vehicle, returning from orbital speeds, must survive the heat of reentry, make its way precisely back to the pad put itself in position to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. The full recovery of an orbital launch system would, in the words of SpaceX, be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" and would open the "door to airplane-like cadence." A successful catch would allow SpaceX to then work on refurbishing Ship for reflight, the next challenge of full reusability. Musk said in August in a SpaceX earnings call that the company will aim to refly the Super Heavy and Ship early next year. SpaceX has a lot of experience with rocket reuse, as its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket pioneered the practice. But the company is eyeing another level of reflight with Starship: It's targeting roughly 10,000 launches of the megarocket per year by 2030, which works out to more than one launch per hour. "We're aiming to reach 30+ Starship launches/day in 2030, which is ~10k annualized," Musk posted on X in August. Why so many launches? The company has repeated that figure to regulators. In comments filed with the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in late October, it said that "SpaceX anticipates conducting 10,000 launches per year itself." Meanwhile, the recently signed National Space Transportation Policy aims to boost the U.S.'s capabilities to support more than 1,000 rocket launches per year by 2030. Musk added that SpaceX's planned Starbase Louisiana site alone could support that many Starship launches. For context: SpaceX launched 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, and that was about half of the global total for orbital flights. Why is SpaceX targeting this incredible increase in launch cadence? It wants to build satellite megaconstellations that dwarf anything the world has ever seen. The company's V3 Starlink satellites are too large to fly efficiently on the Falcon 9. Each one of the next-gen spacecraft adds 1 terabit of capacity to SpaceX's broadband network, and the 26 flying on Flight 15 are equivalent to around 10 Falcon 9 launches packed with Starlink V2 Mini satellites, according to SpaceX. And the company wants to put a staggering 100,000 V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. (There are currently about 11,000 current-gen Starlink satellites in orbit, and that's by far the largest satellite network assembled to date.) SpaceX's Starmind project blows even this figure out of the water. SpaceX wants to launch up to 1 million satellites to serve as orbital AI data centers, and it appears to be making the moves terrestrially regarding the hardware. On Nov. 10, German firm Singulus Technologies announced a contract worth more than 60 million euros for a solar cell production line for Starmind satellites, which SpaceX builds in Bastrop, Texas. Musk said the order covers equipment for 100 gigawatts of solar cells per year. In terms of orbital hardware, the project is only feasible if SpaceX can reach its targeted "airplane-like cadence." The gap The gap between SpaceX's vision and the situation today is vast. Starship flew four times in 2024 and five times in 2025, and Flight 15 would be its fourth launch of 2026. Musk said on the earnings call that he expects Starship to fly weekly at some point in the first half of 2027, and twice weekly or more by the end of that year. Starbase in Texas is currently authorized for 25 launches per year, and the Louisiana site is not expected to host a launch before 2029. Even a perfect outing for Flight 15 and two clean catches will leave lots of work to do. SpaceX will then need to demonstrate reflight with Ship, after assessing the impact on its heat shield system. Then comes orbital refueling , which is a necessary step for any Starship trip beyond LEO and a requirement for SpaceX's commitment to NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. It's unclear how many tanker flights and refuelings will be needed to make a lunar mission possible, but, whatever the number, Starship will probably need to be rapidly reusable. Another step is carrying people. SpaceX has tested life support hardware on the ground in a crew cabin for the moon lander version of Starship that it is building for NASA, but no Starship has flown with such a system. There are no guarantees for Flight 15. Ship will only be cleared for a return to Starbase and a catch attempt if it meets safety checks after reaching orbit, which itself is an achievement not to be taken for granted. Flight controllers may end up needing to bring Ship down in the Pacific Ocean or divert its reentry into the Gulf late into flight. Musk told investors last month that success on this flight is " more likely than not ." Whatever happens today and on Saturday, the measure of Starship's progress will soon shift from whether SpaceX can catch a Ship to how quickly it can launch one again.

item.title: 18th Global ELOY Awards 2026 Unveils Nominees, Celebrating Women Shaping Industries and Driving Change
item.description: The Exquisite Ladies of the Year (ELOY) Awards Foundation has officially announced the nominees for the 18th Global ELOY Awards 2026. This year’s theme, “The Power of Being Seen” recognises exceptional women whose work, leadership, innovation and contributions continue to make an impact across industries and communities. Now in its 18th edition, the Global ELOY Awards continues its commitment to celebrating women who are creating opportunities, building businesses, influencing conversations and contributing to the growth of their respective industries. This year’s nominees represent a diverse range of fields, including fashion, film, beauty, business, technology, media, healthcare, fitness and social impact across Nigeria and beyond. The nominees for the 18th Global ELOY Awards 2026 are: Award category Nominee Business / Brand / Project ELOY Award for Fashion Celebrating an outstanding woman shaping Nigeria/Africa’s fashion industry through design, entrepreneurship, modelling, styling, fashion business or creative direction. Prudent Gabriel Peterson Prudential Atelier Sandrah Tubobereni TUBO Woman Toluwani Wabara Wanni Fuga Yemi Shoyemi Yemi Shoyemi ELOY Award for Creative Economy (Film Producers) Recognising a woman creating economic value through film, music, art, photography, design, content creation, theatre or other creative industries. Blessing Uzzi Call of My Life Laju Iren Onobiren: The Woman’s Story Anita Odiakaose Ikenga: The Last Festival Nora Awolowo & Nicole Ofoegbu Black Market Zulumoke Oyibo Okanjuwa Funmbi Ogunbanwo ELOY Award for Beauty – Retail Celebrating a woman making an exceptional contribution to the beauty industry through entrepreneurship, innovation, artistry, education or brand building. Subuola Oyeleye Beauty Hut Beatrice Eneh Nectar Beauty Hub Hilary Rodriguez-Taiwo Hilary Says Olabisi Odunayo A3 Beauty Mariam Macaulay My Lab Africa Adaeze Atube Thema Beauty Shop Nnenna Okoye Youtopia Beauty Muinat Kosoko Mirrors Beauty ELOY Award for Business Recognising an exceptional female entrepreneur who has built a successful business, created jobs, served customers exceptionally and demonstrated resilience and innovation. Ajoke Amusat The Grocery Lady Biobele Oyibo Earlybean Mariam Grey Pharmacy Jennifer Esiaba Oshin Ayokunlemi Nature Effects Limited Roberta Edu-Oyedokun Moppet Foods ELOY Award for Technology & Innovation Celebrating a woman using technology, digital innovation or new ideas to solve problems, build businesses or transform her industry. Ekwutosi Cynthia Ekeh Digital Witch Sarah Idahosa Women in Defi Ire Aderinokun Bumpa Esther Uzodinma EsteBare Limited Aishat Adama Adamu Rekool Mary-Brenda Akoda GenScan AI Adaeze Ruth Akpagbula Farm Speak Christine Imoukhuede Ahavaplan Toyosi Badejo-Okusanya Adaptive Atelier ELOY Award for Media & Entertainment – On Air Personality Recognising a woman whose work in radio or digital media has captured public attention and created influence. Gloria Babarinde Sarah Ofonedu ifmlago
